newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW - Jardine sees post-97 business as usual.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Jardine sees post-97 business as usual.

text.p: When China's economic tsar shook hands with the chairman of Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd last month, the response in Hong Kong was relief.

The market interpreted the gesture, extended in Beijing by Vice Premier Zhu Rongji to Henry Keswick, chairman of a company once reviled as the "black sheep of business," as an invitation to the colonial trading firm to come in from the cold.
The gesture was a welcome one, Jardine's managing director Alasdair Morrison said on Monday.
But the perception that Jardines had been squeezed out of the Chinese market in the past decade as a result of Beijing displeasure was not true, he told Reuters in an interview.
"I don't think we felt particularly constrained in what we we were able to do in developing our business in China," Morrison said.
The company, Hong Kong's largest private-sector employer, now operates more than 70 joint ventures in China, staffed by more than 15,000 people and generating a turnover of more than US$1 billion.

The British colony of Hong Kong reverts to China in just 29 day's time and Morrison, along with the heads of Hong Kong's main colonial trading firms, is keen to spread the message it will be business as usual in future.
China has promised Hong Kong it can continue its free-wheeling capitalist system independent of the regime in the rest of communist-ruled China after the handover at midnight on June 30.

But the perception still lingers in some quarters that old animosities spell trouble for Jardines, whose roots lie in the opium trade which led to war and the seizing of Hong Kong by the British in 1841.

Jardines angered Beiing when it shifted its domicile out of Hong Kong to Bermuda in 1984, when the ink had barely dried on the Sino-British Joint Declaration, signed that year, governing the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule.

The delisting of the group's companies from the Hong Kong stock exchange in 1994 and 1995 was viewed by China as a case of rats deserting a sinking ship although Jardine clearly stated its disagreement with Hong Kong's stock market listing regulations was the sole reason for the departure.

The stinging black sheep attack came when Beijing stepped in to hold up a high-ticket contract awarded to a consortium led by Jardine to develop the territory's ninth container terminal. Sino-British relations over the transfer of Hong Kong were already strained at the time. Plans by the British to implement mild last minute democratic reforms infuriated China further.
It did not help when a Jardine director defended the plans.
"When you are doing business at a working level, it obviously helps if there is is a sense of friendly cooperation between the parties," Morrison said.

China buried the hatchet and gave the container port the go-ahead late last year, a decision welcomed in Hong Kong where many had fretted about Chinese interference in business and saw tensions as bad for business.
The handshake in Beijing was interpreted as another olive branch.
"The meeting enabled us to reaffirm at a very senior level in China our committment to Hong Kong," Morrison said.
China in turn expressed its assurance that international business would be welcome in Hong Kong -- and China itself -- for years to come.
"Clearly in the past the relationship was not as relaxed and friendly as we hope it will be in the future," Morrison said.
"Now we hope that is all behind us.
